title: CJP Warns Government of Fresh Action Over Delayed FIR Withdrawals Against Protesters
excerpt: After a Supreme Court hearing, the organization accused the Centre of delay tactics and demanded compensation for deceased NEET aspirants.
body:
• CJP spokesperson Saurav Das warned the government of renewed action after a Supreme Court hearing over delays in withdrawing FIRs against NEET student protesters
  • The organization demanded compensation for deceased NEET aspirants and full withdrawal of all protest-related cases across BJP and NDA-ruled states
  • Government had guaranteed FIR withdrawals by a specific deadline but has not delivered written assurances despite weeks of negotiations
  • Supreme Court has directed no coercive action against peaceful protesters while clarifying that states are at liberty to close FIRs

Cockroach Janta Party spokesperson Saurav Das on Monday warned the central government of fresh action over continued delays in withdrawing FIRs against student protesters, speaking to media after a Supreme Court hearing on the matter, according to reports from ABP Live, The Times of India, and The Telegraph.

Das accused the government of playing "delay tactics" and warned that if students are forced to take to the streets again, "it won't be right for the government." He also demanded compensation for deceased NEET aspirants, expanding the CJP's demands beyond FIR withdrawals.

Broken Promises on FIR Withdrawals

The confrontation traces back to late July, when massive student protests erupted across India over the NEET paper leak scandal. The CJP, which spearheaded the agitation, called off its nationwide protests after the government guaranteed that all FIRs filed against students and protesters would be withdrawn — not just in Delhi, but across all BJP and NDA-ruled states.

"The government gave us a guarantee that all FIRs filed against students and protesters so far would be withdrawn and that no action would be taken against any protester in the future."

— Saurav Das, CJP Chief Spokesperson

Das has repeatedly stated that a specific deadline was set for the withdrawals, but weeks later, the government has not provided written assurances. While Bihar and Assam issued notifications promising to withdraw cases and release detained protesters, several other states have not followed suit.

Supreme Court Involvement

The Supreme Court, hearing a batch of petitions related to alleged police excesses during the protests, has issued several key directions. In late July, a bench led by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant ordered no coercive action against peaceful protesters and directed the immediate release of all detained minors without criminal records.

In a subsequent hearing, Solicitor General Tushar Mehta, appearing for Delhi Police, told the court that all FIRs against protesters "can be withdrawn" except against those with criminal antecedents. However, the court's order allowing investigations to continue — even without coercive action — has become a point of contention.

Senior advocate AM Singhvi argued that the term "criminal antecedents" needs clarification, noting that even minor offences like traffic violations or past political protests could be used to deny students protection. "There can be driving offence, some petty offence, political protests. The word needs clarification," he told the bench.

Police Action Under Scrutiny

The protests drew sharp criticism after reports of heavy-handed police action, including the use of lathi charges, tear gas, and pellet rounds against student demonstrators. In one incident in Bihar, an officer was reported to have used an AK-47 weapon during the protests. The Supreme Court has observed that peaceful protests do not justify a lathi charge and is considering an independent probe into allegations of police excesses.

The CJP launched a platform called "Sakshi" where students can submit videos, photographs, and testimonies of alleged police brutality for use as evidence in legal proceedings.

What's Next

The CJP has made clear that it will resume nationwide protests if the government fails to honor its commitments. The case is expected to return before the Supreme Court, where the Centre and state governments may need to explain the gap between their verbal assurances and ground-level action. For millions of Indian students and their families — including those in the diaspora whose children participate in competitive examinations — the outcome will shape the boundaries of protest rights and government accountability in India.
